# Cyber Threats Lurk in Kids' Gaming: What Parents Should Know

### Understand potential risks to help young gamers safely explore exciting worlds online

![A teen boy plays a video game at a laptop in the dark. ](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_large.png)

Video games have long been popular with teenagers, but gaming has become an increasingly dominant part of childhood, with younger kids now gaming more than ever. While gaming offers many benefits, it also comes with genuine risks; understanding these risks can help families set appropriate boundaries and keep kids safe while still enjoying what games have to offer.

The latest [Common Sense Census: Media Use by Kids Zero to Eight](/sites/default/files/research/report/2025-common-sense-census-web-2.pdf) shows that gaming time has increased by 65% since 2020, with children age 8 and under now playing for an average of 38 minutes per day. And it makes sense: Video games have many real benefits for kids, like helping [support creativity](https://www.nyu.edu/about/news-publications/news/2024/may/video-games-can-have-a-positive-impact-on-children---if-designed.html#:~:text=New%20research%20finds%20that%20digital%20games%20can,must%20design%20games%20to%20support%20positive%20outcomes.&text=The%20three%20studies%20found%20that%20games%20can,help%20them%20regulate%20emotions%20and%20build%20relationships) and even [boost cognitive performance](https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/video-gaming-may-be-associated-better-cognitive-performance-children). But as parents and educators navigate this evolving digital landscape, it's important to understand the real risks found in "sandbox" games—open-world games where players can freely explore, create, and interact with others, like Fortnite, Roblox, and Minecraft. Awareness of these risks helps keep both children and the whole family safe, whether they're online or offline.

Like real playgrounds, online games need rules and oversight to protect kids and keep them safe. Modern gaming accounts often collect valuable personal information, saved payment methods, and digital items worth real money. This makes them attractive targets for cybercriminals, leading to financial loss, identity theft, and danger for young gamers.

### **Go Phishing**

Gaming platforms have created their own economies using virtual currencies like V-Bucks (Fortnite), Robux (Roblox), and Minecoins (Minecraft). While these might seem like play money to kids, they have actual cash value and attract sophisticated criminals. In one instance, a user lost [over $2 million worth](https://securelist.com/game-related-threat-report-2023/110960/) of in-app purchases after their account was hacked. While this is an extreme example, even unexpectedly losing $50 can be tough, and victims aren't likely to recoup much of their losses, if any.

When hackers launch *phishing* attacks—which are deceptive attempts to steal personal information by pretending to be trustworthy sources—their goal is to trick players into clicking dangerous links or downloading harmful attachments. **Kids are often targeted with fake links promising free in-game rewards, rare items, or cheat codes** that instead lead to websites that steal account information.For example, scammers create fake sites or apps that claim to offer free or heavily discounted V-Bucks, Robux, or other gaming currencies. When players enter their account details, scammers steal their login credentials.

Once hackers gain access to an account, they typically follow a [common pattern](https://www.allstateidentityprotection.com/business/content-hub/cybercriminals-use-fortnite-to-target-children-bank-accounts) to profit from this theft. They usually start by making unauthorized purchases with any payment methods saved to the account, often buying expensive items or large amounts of in-game currency. These stolen virtual items are quickly transferred to other accounts under their control, making them harder to recover. The criminals then convert these stolen goods into real money by selling virtual items or entire compromised accounts on third-party marketplaces. Finally, they may use the hacked account to send messages to a player's friend list, attempting to spread their scams to more players.

**Think your kids' account may have gotten hacked?** [Read our tips](/articles/what-can-i-do-if-my-kids-device-or-account-has-been-hacked) on what to do next.

### **Dangerous Downloads**

[Recent investigations](https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/internet-security/scam-alert-fake-minecraft-roblox-hacks-on-youtube-hide-malware-target-kids/) have shown that cybercriminals use platforms like YouTube or GitHub to spread *malware*—software designed to damage or steal data from computers—disguised as "game mods" (modifications that change or enhance games). These malicious programs are designed to steal passwords, payment information, and personal data, often targeting more than just gaming accounts. Kids and teens are particularly vulnerable to this because they often lack experience in identifying online scams. The promise of features like "Aimbots" (to improve shooting accuracy) or "Anti-Ban" systems (to avoid getting caught by game administrators) makes these fake downloads even more tempting. Scammers exploit kids' curiosity and eagerness, as they're more likely than adults to take risks without thinking, to trick them into downloading harmful software onto personal or family devices.

![](/sites/default/files/featured-content/avaritia-modfor-minecraft.jpg)

**Since children often use their parents' credit cards for in-game purchases, cybercriminals target them to obtain payment details or personal data that can be exploited to** [**commit fraud**](https://www.experian.com/blogs/insights/online-gaming-fraud/) **or can be** [**sold on the** ***dark web***](https://www.securitymagazine.com/articles/93226-stolen-fortnite-accounts-reportedly-earn-hackers-millions-per-year)**.** The connected nature of today's gaming creates additional security risks. Many players reuse passwords across multiple platforms, or link their gaming accounts to social media, which means a single breach can potentially give hackers access to multiple accounts. In 2023, hackers used a type of malware called [SpyNote](https://securelist.com/game-related-threat-report-2023/110960/) to target Roblox players by disguising it as a game mod. Once installed, this malware could secretly track everything typed on the keyboard, record the screen, and access the device's camera. It could even mimic official Google and Facebook apps to deceive users into revealing their passwords.

### **When Online Dangers Go Offline**

One of the most serious risks in online gaming goes beyond in-game scams or hacked accounts—it's the possibility of [children interacting with predators](https://ussafe.org/children-and-online-predators/) who use these platforms to target young users. Online multiplayer games allow kids to chat with friends *and* strangers. And while most of these players may be harmless, some have far more dangerous intentions.

![](/sites/default/files/featured-content/chatfeature.jpg)

**Predators build trust by connecting with kids through games, and then move kids to less moderated apps. This tactic, known as** ***grooming*****, is designed to isolate young users from trusted adults.** In some cases, this escalates to [sextortion](https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/nashville/news/sextortion-a-growing-threat-targeting-minors), where predators pressure kids into sharing personal information or explicit images by using threats and manipulation, and then demand payment to keep from sharing this content with others. These risks aren't just [hypothetical](https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2024-roblox-pedophile-problem/)—the anonymity of gaming platforms makes it easier for predators to blend in. And because these conversations often happen outside of parental supervision, kids may not recognize red flags until they're already in a dangerous situation that can lead to [tragic outcomes](https://www.usatoday.com/story/life/health-wellness/2025/02/25/teenage-boys-mental-health-suicide-sextortion-scams/78258882007/).

While these risks are real and important to recognize, they shouldn't prevent kids and families from enjoying gaming and online interactions altogether. Knowledge truly is power, and education is your best defense against potential dangers. By staying informed, setting boundaries, and communicating openly, families can confidently navigate digital spaces—ensuring that the fun continues without compromising safety.

### **How Kids and Parents Can Stay Safe**

**For Kids: Protect Your Gaming Experience**

* **Never share login details**: If someone claiming to be from a game company asks for your password, it's almost certainly a scam. Even if the request looks legit, real developers have alternative verification methods that don't involve you sharing your password.
* **Avoid "too good to be true" deals**: Free currency generators and hacks are almost always scams. When in doubt, [take nine seconds to think](https://pausetake9.org/) before clicking.
* **Stick to official stores and downloads**: Only download games, mods, and software from official websites or app stores.
* **Report suspicious behavior**: If someone asks for personal information or tries to lure you to an outside website, report them through the game's official moderation tools ([Roblox](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/203312410-How-to-Report-Rule-Violations), [Fortnite](https://safety.epicgames.com/en-US/policies/reporting-misconduct), [Minecraft](https://help.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/request/new?ticket_form_id=4416074743565)) and tell a trusted adult.
* **Enable two-factor authentication (2FA)**: [Many gaming platforms](https://2fa.directory/us/#gaming) offer this extra layer of security—like requiring a code from a cellphone—to prevent unauthorized access.

**For Parents: Keep Your Child's Gaming Safe**

* **Use parental controls:** [Many platforms offer settings](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/positively-media/202311/how-and-why-to-use-parental-controls-in-video-games) to limit in-game purchases, prevent interactions with strangers, and even filter out inappropriate language in chat.
* **Monitor purchases and account activity:** Keep an eye on in-game transactions to prevent unauthorized spending.
* **Build digital literacy:** Help your child think critically about what they see. Discuss why some content is inappropriate, and how to spot warning signs.
* **Review games together:** Check the games your child has recently played and talk about any content that doesn't seem age-appropriate. Our [family tech planners](/family-tech-planners) can help inspire conversations about what kinds of games, devices, and sites are appropriate.
* **Encourage open communication:** Let your kid know they can talk with you about anything uncomfortable that they experience. (It may help to reassure them that you won't stop them from playing altogether.)
* **Teach kids to spot red flags:** Explain to your child that if someone asks to chat on another app or platform, or if they request personal details, these are red flags. Helping your child understand why we don't share personal information like full names, school details, or phone numbers can keep everyone safe.
* **Take control of your family's digital security:** [Get step-by-step guidance and personalized recommendations](https://securityplanner.consumerreports.org/) from our friends at Consumer Reports to secure your online accounts, devices, and personal information, helping you reduce cyber risks and strengthen your digital safety.

**Ready to dive deeper?** Check out our Parents' Ultimate Guides on [Roblox](/articles/parents-ultimate-guide-to-roblox), [Fortnite](/articles/parents-ultimate-guide-to-fortnite), and [Minecraft](/articles/parents-ultimate-guide-to-minecraft) to learn more about these popular online games.

**Share your story**. If your family has had an experience involving hacking, phishing, or other cyber crimes that you are comfortable sharing with us, please fill out [this form](https://forms.gle/iM5Wn4kUR3XgiBkq8) or send us a note at [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#1972707d6a787a6d707677597a76747476776a7c776a7c37766b7e). These stories help us in our work to make the internet and online gaming safer and healthier for all kids.

# Parents' Ultimate Guide to Roblox

![blue and green abstract shapes](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_large.png)

## Parents Need to Know

* Roblox doesn't have strict age restrictions, so kids under 13 can play alongside teens and adults. With so many players and an endless number of games, not all games are suitable for young children, and some inappropriate content can get through the age filters.
* Following safety concerns, Roblox is rolling out new protections for under-13 users in November and December 2024. These updates include mandatory age ratings for games, limits on social spaces, and restrictions on unmoderated content. Since these changes are new and won't be fully enforced until 2025, we're not sure what their impact will be.
* Roblox has social features like text chat and voice chat in some games. While these features encourage social interaction, they also open the door to kids talking to people they don't know and possibly cyberbullying.
* Roblox encourages spending on its virtual currency, "Robux," through limited-time events, exclusive items, and social pressure. Many platforms like this use "freemium" features, where spending money enhances the experience, so it's important to set boundaries early on.
* With the right supervision and guidance, Roblox can be a positive experience for kids. It offers creative opportunities through game design, coding, and teamwork. Parents can make the most of these features by managing safety settings and keeping an open dialogue about online behavior.

* [What is Roblox?](#section-0)
* [Key Concerns and Solutions](#section-1)
* [Age-by-Age Guide](#section-2)

![purple blob ](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_medium.png)

## What is Roblox?

Roblox isn't a singular game— it's a huge online platform where users play, create, and share hundreds of thousands of games. It's like a virtual playground where players use Lego-style characters (called avatars) to explore millions of games created by other users. These games range from adopting pets to solving mysteries to running a pizza shop. With over 70 million daily players—including 32 million under age 13—Roblox has become a big part of kids' digital lives.

### Is it free?

Yes, the basic platform is free to download and play. But keep in mind, Roblox uses a virtual currency called "Robux," which costs real money. Many players, especially impressionable kids, can feel pressure to buy Robux for avatar upgrades, special abilities, and premium features in games.

### Where do kids play it?

Kids can play Roblox on almost any device, including phones, tablets, computers, Xbox and PlayStation consoles, and VR headsets, making it easy to access anywhere.

### Is there an age requirement?

Roblox doesn't have a strict age minimum, but it does use different ratings for game content:

* **All Ages**: Mild content, light fantasy violence.
* **9+**: May include more fantasy violence.
* **13+**: Contains more intense content and social interactions.
* **17+**: Mature content, requiring age verification.

While these Roblox experience ratings aim to guide users toward age-appropriate games, it's possible for inappropriate content to slip through. The ratings primarily focus on violence and may not fully cover other areas like sexual content, drug use, or crude humor.

![yellow blob](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_medium.png) [Back to top](#pug-view-links)

## Key Concerns and Solutions

### What are Robux, and How Do I Manage In-Game Spending?

Robux is Roblox's virtual currency, and it's at the heart of most parent-child conflicts on the platform. While Roblox is free to download, the platform heavily promotes Robux purchases for everything from virtual clothing to special game features. Kids face constant pressure to buy items, especially during limited-time events or when their friends have premium items.

Kids can get Robux in a few ways:

* **Direct purchase**: Robux can be bought online through Roblox with a credit card or PayPal.
* **Gift cards**: Roblox gift cards are available at most major retailers and provide a set amount of Robux.
* **Roblox Premium**: This monthly subscription gives users a Robux allowance and extra perks.
* **Earning**: Older users can earn Robux by creating games or items that other players buy.

**What You Can Do:**

* **Set spending rules**: Establish clear monthly limits on Robux, or tie purchases to chores or an allowance.
* **Avoid linking credit cards**: Use Roblox gift cards instead of linking a payment method to avoid surprise charges.
* **Watch for scams**: Let your child know that any offer of "free Robux" is a scam.
* **Track spending together**: Check the purchase history regularly and talk to your child about smart spending choices.
* **Use in-game parental controls: You can set** [**monthly spending restrictions**](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/4409125091348-Monthly-Spend-Restrictions)**, receive** [**spend notifications**](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/4409139163412-Spend-Notifications-Controls)**, and set up a** [**parent pin**](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/360031680051-How-Do-I-Add-Change-or-Remove-a-PIN)**.**

### How Do I Keep My Kid Safe from Inappropriate Content?

Because Roblox is user-generated, kids may still run into inappropriate content despite the platform's safety filters. This includes "condo games" (which usually feature adult themes and sexual content), violent games, gambling-style play, and even games that may have bullying or hate speech.

Roblox offers experience ratings (All Ages, 9+, 13+, and 17+), but they aren't perfect. Even "All Ages" games can have user-generated elements that slip through moderation. Starting in December 2024, Roblox will require stricter age labels for games and will restrict certain free-form content for younger users. It's still unclear how effective these updates will be.

**What You Can Do:**

* **Use safety features as a starting point**: Enable [account restrictions](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/360000375686-Account-Restrictions) and set filters for age-appropriate games. You don't want to rely on these restrictions alone, but you do want to talk to kids about why you're setting restrictions, reminding them it's for protection and not punishment.
* **Review games together**: Check the games your child has recently played and talk about any content that doesn't seem age-appropriate.
* **Build digital literacy**: Help your child think critically about what they see, discussing why some content is inappropriate and how to spot warning signs.
* **Encourage open communication**: Let your kid know they can talk to you about anything uncomfortable that they experience. (It may help to reassure them that you won't stop them from playing Roblox altogether.)
* **Make reporting a habit**: Show them how to use [Roblox's Report Abuse feature](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/203312410-How-to-Report-Rule-Violations#:~:text=To%20report%20an%20entire%20experience,on%20the%20experience's%20About%20page.) and explain that reporting helps keep the community safer for everyone.

### Is It Safe for My Kid to Chat with Other Players on Roblox?

Roblox's chat features make it easy for kids to connect with friends, but they also allow interactions with strangers. While Roblox uses filters to block inappropriate language in text and voice conversations, some users find ways around these filters, and this moderation may even encourage kids to continue conversations on other platforms where monitoring is limited. Starting November 18, 2024, Roblox will stop kids under 13 from entering "Social Hangouts"—spaces designed for chatting—with the goal of reducing unmonitored interactions. Parents should be mindful that [cyberbullying](/node/84823) can still occur in these spaces, whether it's directed at your child or comes from your child, so it's important to stay involved and aware by having conversations with kids about their online behavior and how to react to others.

**What You Can Do**:

* **Adjust chat settings**: [Chat and privacy filters](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/203313120-Safety-Features-Chat-Privacy-Filtering) are your best friend. For younger kids and even tweens and teens, consider setting chat to "friends only" or turning it off completely. This helps ensure that only trusted people can reach them.
* **Teach kids to spot red flags**: Explain to your child that if someone asks to chat on another app or platform, or if they request personal details, these are red flags. Remind them that they can always come to you or another trusted adult if they feel unsure or uncomfortable.
* **Review their friends list together**: Regularly check who your child is connected with on Roblox, and talk to them about only adding people they know in real life. You can also talk to them about having access to their account so you can [see who they're interacting with](https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/360031384652-How-can-I-see-what-my-child-is-doing-on-Roblox).
* **Discuss why privacy matters**: Help your child understand why we don't share personal information like full names, school details, or phone numbers. Remind them that keeping certain information private helps keep them safe.

![green blob](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_medium.png) [Back to top](#pug-view-links)

## Age-by-Age Guide

### Younger Kids (5–7)

Kids this age are excited by Roblox's creative and imaginative play, but they need hands-on guidance to keep their experience safe and fun.

**What to Expect**:

* Fascination with games and pets, but limited understanding of online risks.
* Strong reactions to wins/losses and first attempts at social play.

**Safety Steps**:

* **Ensure that their account is set up as under age 13**. Many of the platform's safety features won't work otherwise.
* **Use strict settings**: Disable chat, or limit it to approved friends.
* **Make sure kids play in family spaces** where you can keep an eye on them.
* **Manage all friend requests** for your child.

**Conversation Starters & Activities**:

* Invite them to share their excitement while you learn what they enjoy most. *"What's the most fun part of playing with your Roblox pet?"*
* Play together to show interest and build trust. *"Can you teach me how to play your favorite game?"*
* **Activity**: Ask them to show you how they play, or try creating a character together. This lets them guide the experience while you stay involved.

### Tweens (8–12)

Tweens are more socially aware and often focus on connecting with friends and building a unique digital identity on Roblox.

**What to Expect**:

* Interest in group play and peer influence over in-game purchases.
* Desire for more independence in choosing games and spending Robux.

**Safety Steps**:

* **Ensure that their account is set up as under age 13**. Many of the platform's safety features won't work otherwise.
* **Review game ratings and set spending limits**.
* **Check friend connections** and discuss online safety.

**Conversation Starters & Activities**:

* Give them a chance to share their judgment process, which you can help build upon. *"How do you decide which games are worth playing?"*
* Let them proudly share something they're excited about. (This can open the door to safety discussions if needed.) *"Show me the coolest thing you've made or done on Roblox lately!"*
* **Activity**: Ask them to walk you through how they pick games or to show you how they customize their avatar. Showing interest in their creative choices lets them know you care about what they enjoy.

### Teens (13+)

Teens are exploring more complex features, and are often interested in developing their own games or further shaping their digital identities. They may want to make their own decisions, but they will still benefit from your guidance on healthy digital habits.

**Safety Steps**:

* **Discuss** [**digital citizenship**](https://www.commonsense.org/education/digital-citizenship?adgroupid=166328656249&adid=702858246890&campaignid=21383101157&gad_source=1&gclid=CjwKCAiAudG5BhAREiwAWMlSjBzgj1Dgs0JHZD3x2AZW62v5Y_bVvVhGsiKUx0OvGAKx-pSShVp-DBoCHqoQAvD_BwE) **and online reputation**.
* **Review privacy settings** and set screen time/spending boundaries.

**Conversation Starters & Activities**:

* Give insight into their creativity and goals. This allows you to support and guide them. *"What would you create if you made your own Roblox game?"*
* Start a natural conversation about trust, online safety, and personal boundaries—without making it feel like a lecture. *"What's something you've learned about other players online?"*
* **Activity**: Ask them to walk you through their game creation process or a project they're proud of. Being a sounding board for their ideas can help build a deeper connection and show them you're genuinely interested.

# Parents' Ultimate Guide to Discord

![blue and green abstract shapes](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_large.png)

## Parents Need to Know

* **Discord isn't just for gaming.** Teens use it to chat, study, and explore interests—but user-moderated spaces mean that content and interactions can get risky.
* **Predatory behavior and harmful content do happen.** Teens have been exposed to sexual content, hate speech, grooming attempts, and toxic ideologies. Safety settings help, but open conversations matter more.
* **There's no real age verification.** Teens can bypass protections by entering a fake birth date. Tools like Family Center help, but open communication works better than silent monitoring.
* **Spending pressure is real.** Teens may feel left out without Nitro or server perks. Set expectations before gift cards or payment methods are linked.
* **It's not just about safety—it's emotional too.** Help your teen notice when Discord feels overwhelming, and remind them it's OK to take breaks or step away.
* **Stay connected, even if you're not on the app.** Ask what servers they're into, how it makes them feel, and help bring online interests into the real world.

* [What is Discord?](#section-0)
* [Safety Features and Settings](#section-1)
* [Key Concerns and Solutions](#section-2)
* [Age-by-Age Guide](#section-3)
* [Making the Most of Discord](#section-4)
* [A Note to Parents](#section-5)

![purple blob ](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_medium.png)

## What is Discord?

Discord is a communication app that started as a way for gamers to talk while playing. Today, it's expanded into a popular place for anyone to connect over shared interests, whether that's gaming, music, anime, art, studying, or any other interest you can imagine.

Instead of a public feed or algorithm, Discord is made up of user-created spaces called **servers**, which are like themed chat rooms. Each server can have multiple **channels** for text, voice, and video chats.

Teens tend to like Discord because it feels more personal and community-driven than other social apps. They can choose which servers to join and chat in real time with friends or others who share their hobbies. It's also become a go-to place for school collaboration, creative projects, and even homework help through official servers hosted by schools or organizations.

As with many online platforms, especially those built around real-time chat, Discord comes with serious risks—especially for younger users. There's been plenty of backlash against the platform for not doing enough to protect minors from harmful content and interactions. While it can be a fun and supportive space when used responsibly, it also allows access to unmoderated servers, private messaging, and content that's not always appropriate for teens or tweens.

### How does Discord work?

Discord organizes communication into servers (communities), channels (topic-specific spaces within servers), and direct messages (private conversations).

### Main Features

**Servers:** These are communities based on shared interests or friend groups. Teens often join multiple servers focused on things like games, music, or fan content. While Discord prohibits harmful content, moderation is usually left to users, which means inappropriate or unfiltered conversations can slip through.

**Channels:** Each server is broken into channels: text channels (marked with a #) and voice channels (marked with 🔊). Teens use them to chat about specific topics or hang out while gaming. Channel names often reflect the content—keep an eye out for terms like "NSFW" or "mature" that may signal inappropriate material.

**Direct messages (DMs):** DMs are private chats between users, and they're where the most concerning interactions can happen. Teens often move from server conversations to DMs for more personal or one-on-one chats. You can adjust settings to limit who can send messages to your teen.

**Voice and video calls:** Live audio or video chats can happen in channels or in DMs. Teens use these to game, study, or hang out casually, often dropping in and out like a group call that's always open. These calls aren't monitored or recorded by Discord, and your teen might be chatting with people they don't know in real life.

**Go live / screen sharing:** Teens can stream their screen to friends or a whole server, usually to show a game, video, or tutorial. Remind them to close other apps first to avoid accidentally revealing private info, like emails or personal documents.

**File sharing:** Teens often share memes, art, or schoolwork through Discord. While Discord now blurs potentially sensitive media by default, the filters aren't foolproof, so it's important to talk to your teen about what's OK to share and what's not.

### Social Features

These tools make Discord feel interactive and fun, but they're mostly on by default and easy for teens to use. While some settings can limit how they work, most of these features aren't easily turned off—so it's important to talk with your teen about how they use them and who they're talking to.

**@mentions:** Teens use @ to tag friends and make sure their message gets noticed. Receiving a notification helps them stay connected—but can also create pressure to respond right away, especially in busy servers, or can be used in cyberbullying.

**Roles:** Roles control what someone can do in a server, like posting in certain channels, adding new members, or deleting content. In small friend servers, teens often create fun or silly roles like "DJ" or "Vibe Checker." In larger servers, roles are more serious and can include moderator permissions, which means that teens could be responsible for managing user behavior or inappropriate content.

**Bots:** Bots are automated tools that can play music, manage polls, or help organize server activity. Most are harmless, but some bots can be misused or link to inappropriate content, so it's worth checking which ones are active in your teen's servers.

**Status updates:** Teens can set a custom status or let Discord automatically show what game they're playing. These updates may seem minor, but they can reveal your teen's activity, availability, or mood to others—sometimes more than they realize.

### Is Discord free?

Yes, Discord's core features like messaging, voice and video calls, and joining servers are all free. But there are several ways for teens to spend money on the platform, and many feel social pressure to do so.

Teens can use credit cards, PayPal, or mobile payment services to make purchases. Discord gift cards are easy to find in stores, which means that teens may spend without needing to connect a parent's payment method.

Discord doesn't offer specific parental controls for purchases, and there's no way to directly limit spending or require approval within the app. That's why it's important to talk with your teen before they buy gift cards or link any payment info to their account.

* **Discord Nitro** **($9.99/month or $99.99/year)**: Nitro is the most common upgrade. It unlocks perks like better video quality, larger file uploads, custom emojis, and animated profiles. Teens often feel pressure to subscribe when friends have Nitro badges or exclusive features.
* **Server boosting ($4.99 per boost)**: Boosts give a server perks like enhanced audio, banners, and custom emojis. Some teens take turns boosting group servers to keep perks active. Boosters often get shout-outs or special roles, which can create pressure to spend.
* **Creator subscriptions:** Many creators use Discord to offer perks to paying fans, like exclusive chat access or early content. Teens may feel obligated to subscribe to support their favorite influencers or to stay part of the community.
* **Server marketplaces:** Some servers now sell digital products or offer paid memberships for access to exclusive channels, roles, or content. These purchases are highly visible and can create pressure for teens to spend in order to access premium spaces or content tied to their interests.
* **In-game spending:** Discord doesn't sell games anymore, but it integrates with platforms like Steam and Xbox. When teens see what their friends are playing, they may feel pressure to buy games or in-game items to join in.

### Is there an age requirement?

Yes. According to Discord's Terms of Service, **users must be** **at least 13 years old**—in line with U.S. privacy laws (COPPA). But there's no real age verification beyond entering a birth date, so younger kids can easily sign up if they lie about their age.

For teens age 13 to 17, Discord turns on some safety features by default, including:

* Blocking direct messages from people they don't know
* Hiding age-restricted servers and NSFW (not safe for work) content
* Blurring sensitive images, and showing alerts when receiving messages from new contacts
* Marking the app as 17+ on iOS—though younger teens can still download and use it

These tools can help, but they work best when **you and your teen set them up together** and talk through why certain settings matter. Still, it's important to know that Discord isn't designed specifically for teens. There's no separate "kids mode," and 13-year-olds are basically using the same version of the app as adults—just with a few safety settings that can be changed.

Every kid is different, and you know yours best. Some teens may be ready to use Discord with guidance and support. Others might need more time to build the skills that help them stay safe and make good choices online, like knowing how to handle messages from strangers, avoid risky content, or manage screen time.

If your child is under 13, it's worth exploring platforms made for younger users that offer built-in parental controls and safer, more age-appropriate spaces.

## Safety Features and Settings

Discord has added more safety tools in recent years, but they still don't offer the same level of control or protection you'll find on platforms designed for younger users. Many settings are optional, easy to change, and rely on your teen using them responsibly. Here's what's available—along with what works, what doesn't, and where to stay alert.

### Privacy & Safety Settings

To access these settings, have your teen tap their profile picture (bottom right corner), then select "Privacy & Safety." These options help control who can contact them and how explicit content is filtered.

* **Safe direct messaging**: Filters explicit content in private messages. Options include:
  + *Keep Me Safe* – Scans all direct messages (DMs).
  + *My Friends Are Nice* – Scans only messages from non-friends.
  + *Do Not Scan* – Disables filtering entirely.

Teens can change these settings at any time. There's no way to lock or require a PIN for this section.

* **Friend request settings**: Lets teens limit who can send them friend requests: *Everyone*, *Friends of Friends*, or *Server Members*. Choosing *Friends of Friends* can reduce unwanted contact. Note that teens can switch this back to *Everyone*. If they're in a public server, they may still receive requests from strangers inside that space.
* **Server privacy defaults**: Lets you disable direct messages from people in newly joined servers. This setting applies only to future servers. Your teen can choose to allow DMs on a server-by-server basis.
* **Sensitive content filters**: Automatically blurs images and videos that may be graphic or explicit. This setting is easy to turn off, and filters can miss inappropriate text or toxic behavior in chats.

For step-by-step guidance to set up these controls, visit the [Discord Safety Center](https://discord.com/safety).

### Teen Safety Assist Features

Aimed at teen accounts, these features are turned on by default for under-18 accounts:

* Safety alerts appear when you receive a message from a new contact.
* An "Ignore" feature lets teens stop seeing messages from someone without alerting that person. Unlike blocking—which cuts off communication completely and notifies the other user if they try to message—the ignore option simply hides the conversation on the teen's end, creating a low-pressure way of taking space.
* Content is automatically filtered for potentially inappropriate images or video.
* Message request controls allow you to limit DMs from strangers.

These settings can be turned off at any time. Teens can also avoid them altogether by signing up with a fake birth date, since Discord doesn't verify age.

### Family Center

Family Center is Discord's only tool for parents. It provides limited insights but does not allow you to change settings or block features.

What you can see:

* Who your teen is messaging (but not the content in the messages)
* Which servers they've joined
* New friends added
* Voice call activity (but not the calls themselves)

**How to set it up**:

1. Download the Discord app on your phone
2. Open the Discord app and go to User Settings > Family Center > Enable Family Center
3. Have your teen generate a QR code on their device
4. Use your phone to scan the QR code, which will link your account with theirs

It's important to know that in order to use Family Center, your teen has to opt in, and they can leave Family Center at any time without notice. The activity history that parents and caregivers can see is limited to the past seven days. And there's no access to the content they're sending or seeing, no alert system, and no setting controls included.

### Reporting Tools

Discord has built-in tools to report harmful content, users, or servers. [To report](https://discord.com/safety/reporting.), click the three dots (⋯) next to a message, select "Report," and follow the prompts. Discord enforces rules against bullying, harassment, and threats, but response times can vary.

Encourage your teen to also tell a trusted adult if something serious happens. Reporting to both Discord and an adult helps make sure they get support no matter what.

### Making Settings More Effective

Settings are just the beginning—they work best when paired with open, ongoing conversations. To help them work for your family:

* **Explore settings together**: Walk through each one with your teen. Ask questions and explain your thinking as you go.
* **Create a family media agreement**: Outline expectations for how, when, and why your teen uses Discord. Revisit it as they become more mature and show responsibility.
* **Check in regularly**: Use feature updates or new interests as natural times to review settings—not just when there's a problem.
* **Focus on support, not surveillance**: Frame settings as tools that support your teen's safety and well-being, not as punishments.
* **Model healthy digital habits**: Show the same boundaries and thoughtful tech use you want your teen to practice. And don't be afraid to make mistakes and show them how to bounce back. It's about practice, not perfection.

## Key Concerns and Solutions

### How Can I Protect My Child from Predators on Discord?

Because Discord is built around shared-interest communities, teens and adults can end up in the same spaces, especially in large public servers. This opens the door to potentially risky interactions. While these worst-case scenarios are not common, law enforcement has documented cases of adults using Discord to groom minors, often starting with casual chats in public servers and moving to private messages over time.

That's why it's important to understand the risks—but also to approach safety through support, not fear. Teens are more likely to come to you if they know you're there to help, not punish. The goal is to build your teen's awareness and confidence in recognizing red flags, while staying involved and informed about how they use the platform.

**What to Watch For:** 

* Friend requests or direct messages from strangers.
* Conversations that turn personal too quickly—especially about appearance, emotions, or relationships.
* Requests to keep chats secret from parents or trusted adults.
* Pressure to move to another platform (like Snapchat or Instagram) or join a private call.
* Offers of gifts, gaming currency, or other rewards.
* Personal questions about your teen's routine, school, or when they're home alone.
* Changes in behavior—like becoming more secretive about online activity.

**What You Can Do:** 

* **Adjust friend request settings** to "Friends of Friends" instead of "Everyone."
* **Limit direct messages** to come only from friends.
* **Turn on "Keep Me Safe"** in Privacy & Safety to filter explicit content.
* **Use Family Center** to see who your teen is chatting with (note: you won't see message content).
* **Talk about red flags**: Help your teen understand what grooming can look like, and encourage them to come to you if something feels off (and to always trust their gut feeling).
* **Create a family agreement** about what personal info is OK to share (and what's not).
* **Remind them that real friends respect boundaries** and won't ask for secrecy.
* **Encourage ignoring or blocking strangers**—and let them know it's OK to say no, even if someone seems nice.
* **Teach them how to report** suspicious users directly to Discord's Trust & Safety team.

### What Should I Know About the Content My Teen Might See on Discord?

Discord hosts thousands of communities for virtually any interest imaginable. While many servers provide positive spaces for connection, teens may come across harmful or inappropriate content ranging from mild to serious, including sexual images, violent or graphic content, discussions of drugs and alcohol, hate speech, or manipulative ideologies.

Even in spaces that start out friendly, the tone can shift quickly. Some communities may share manipulative or extreme messaging, like content that promotes hate, reinforces gender stereotypes, or frames relationships and power in unhealthy ways. These ideas can show up gradually through jokes, memes, or conversations, which is why helping your teen build awareness, trust, and digital judgment is often more effective than trying to shield them from everything. 

**What to Watch For:** 

* Servers labeled "NSFW" or "age-restricted" in their descriptions.
* Channels with age warnings (these should be blocked automatically for users under 18).
* Gaming communities centered around M-rated or violent games.
* Sudden screen switching or app closing when you walk by.
* Not wanting to talk about which servers they're in.
* Late-night use when they think you're not paying attention.

**What You Can Do:** 

* Turn on the "Keep Me Safe" content filter in Privacy & Safety settings.
* Make sure your teen's birth date is accurate in their account so age-based filters work.
* Enable Teen Safety Assist, which automatically blurs potentially graphic media.
* Create a judgment-free space where your teen feels safe talking about what they see, and be open to answering questions and not shaming.
* For younger teens, set an expectation that if they want to join a new server, they need to have a quick check-in with a trusted adult.
* Help them discover well-moderated servers focused on their real interests, like art, coding, books, or creative projects.
* Focus on critical thinking skills so they can make smart choices in the moment, even when filters don't catch everything.
* Check in and follow up past the moment they come in contact with disturbing content.

### How Do I Stay Involved in My Teen's Discord Use Without Invading Their Privacy?

Finding the right balance between keeping your teen safe and respecting their independence can be tricky. This is especially true on platforms like Discord, where much of the interaction happens in private messages or voice chats that can't be easily seen or reviewed.

While it's natural to want insight into what your teen is doing online, surveillance can backfire—especially if it leads to secrecy or shuts down communication. Instead of focusing on control, aim to create an environment where your teen feels safe coming to you with questions, concerns, or mistakes.

**What to Watch For:** 

* Increased secretiveness about online activities.
* Password-protecting devices that weren't secured before.
* Minimizing screens when you enter the room.
* Using Discord at unusual hours.
* Emotional changes after using Discord.

**What You Can Do:** 

* Set up Family Center to see who your teen is messaging without reading their conversations.
* Have open conversations about online safety, rather than secret monitoring.
* Create a family Discord server where you can also participate and see how the platform works.
* Ask your teen to show you their server list without reading their private messages
* Establish tech-free times and zones in your home.
* Focus monitoring efforts on when and how much they use Discord, rather than monitoring specific conversations.
* Consider using device-level parental controls for younger teens that set time limits rather than spying on content.

### What Are the Signs My Teen Might be Struggling with Something They've Seen or Experienced in Discord?

While Discord can be a great space for connection, creativity, and belonging, it can also expose teens to bullying, harassment, or emotionally difficult content, sometimes in subtle ways that build up over time. Conversations in public servers or private messages may include toxic behavior, peer pressure, or exposure to issues like self-harm, disordered eating, or hate speech.

Repeated exposure to negative online interactions—even ones that seem minor at first—can impact a teen's self-esteem, mood, and sense of safety. Sometimes, teens don't immediately connect their emotional struggles to what's happening online, especially if they're being told it's "just a joke" or if they fear losing access to their digital spaces.

That's why it's important to stay tuned in to emotional changes and create a space where your teen feels safe sharing what they're experiencing, without fear of punishment or judgment. Early conversations and supportive guidance can go a long way in preventing more serious harm.

**What to Watch For:** 

* Increased anxiety, sadness, irritability, or withdrawal-like symptoms.
* Sleep issues, appetite changes, or unexplained physical complaints.
* Avoiding school or activities they used to enjoy.
* Sudden changes in how they use Discord—like deleting the app or leaving servers without explanation.
* Emotional shifts after being online, like shutting down or getting upset after using Discord.
* Becoming secretive about online activity or quickly switching screens.
* Self-disparaging comments like "no one likes me," "I'm so stupid," or "I mess everything up"—especially when said more frequently, with intensity, or after using Discord.
* Declining performance in school or disinterest in friendships.
* Talking about self-harm or feeling hopeless (always take this seriously and seek professional support right away; see below).

**What You Can Do:** 

* **Create regular, low-pressure check-ins** where your teen can talk about what's happening online—both the good and the hard.
* **Ask open-ended questions** like "What's your favorite server right now?" or "Have you ever seen something in a chat that didn't feel right?"
* **Teach them how to use Discord's safety tools** (like blocking, reporting, or using the Ignore feature) and when to use them.
* **Encourage saving screenshots** of harmful messages in case something needs to be reported.
* **Remind them they deserve respect** in every environment—online and offline.
* **Validate their emotions**, even if you don't understand why something online feels upsetting.
* **If bullying involves classmates**, consider working with school staff or counselors—while including your teen in decisions about how to move forward.
* **Report serious or persistent harm** to Discord's Trust & Safety team and authorities.
* **Seek professional mental health support** if your teen shows signs of distress, withdrawal, or talks about self-harm. You can always reach out to:
* **National Crisis Hotline**: Call or text **988**
* **Crisis Text Line**: Text **HOME** to **741741**
* **Your child's health care provider or school counselor** for guidance, referrals, or support plans
* **Remind your teen that their well-being comes first**—no digital space is worth their mental health.

## Age-by-Age Guide

Every child develops differently, and what works for one child might not work for another. The following guidelines offer age-based suggestions based on typical developmental stages, but you know your child best. Use these recommendations as a starting point, and adjust based on your child's maturity level and interests as well as your family values.

### Tweens (8–12)

**What to Expect:** 

At this age, tweens are curious and eager to connect—especially if older siblings, family members, or favorite influencers are using Discord. But they're also more impulsive, more trusting of strangers, and not yet equipped to recognize manipulation, social pressure, or risky content. Even simple exposure to group chats or messages meant for older users can be emotionally confusing or upsetting.

**Safety Approach:** 

Based on the platform's terms and child privacy laws, kids under 13 shouldn't be on Discord. If your child is already using it:

* Stay calm and have a curious, non-judgmental conversation.
* Explain why some platforms have age limits—and that it's about safety, not punishment.
* Ask them what they like about it and offer safer alternatives like Messenger Kids or supervised game chats.
* If you allow limited use, restrict their communication to private family or real-life friend servers, and monitor activity closely.
* Keep devices in common areas and turn off direct messages (DMs) from server members.

**Conversation Starters & Activities:** 

* To understand what they're hoping to get out of using Discord: *"Are your friends talking about Discord? What sounds fun about it to you?"*
* To connect with their interest while explaining age limits: *"It makes sense that you'd want to use what your friends are using. Can we talk about why some apps have age limits—and figure out together what you can use now that feels just as fun?"*
* **Activity:** Create a "grown-up tech challenge" together—like a checklist of digital habits they can practice to build trust and show they're getting ready for older platforms. Include things like asking before downloading new apps, taking screen breaks, or talking about tricky moments online.

### Younger Teens (13–14)

**What to Expect:** 

At this age, teens are starting to explore their social identities and crave more independence online. Discord's group chats, friend servers, and shared-interest communities feel exciting, but they may not yet recognize manipulation, peer pressure, or emotionally harmful environments. Because they're still developing emotional regulation and critical thinking, what happens in a chat can stick with them, even if they don't talk about it.

**Safety Approach:**

This is a great time to help your teen build digital habits that support emotional safety—not just avoid danger.

* Go through privacy settings together and talk about what they *actually do* and what digital dilemmas they can help prevent. Connect it to reality instead of making it abstract.
* Help them decide how they want to feel when they use Discord—and how to spot when it stops feeling fun or safe.
* Encourage them to choose servers that reflect who they are or who they want to become, and what their interests are. (Not just what's popular or where their friends are.) Go through some servers together to practice.
* Make space to talk about moments that feel off, like a joke that made them uncomfortable, someone asking personal questions too fast, or being left out of a conversation. Even if they're not sure why it bothered them, help them name that feeling.
* If they're feeling overwhelmed or hurt, show them how to use features like the Ignore tool to take space—without drama or escalation.
* For now, it's still a good idea to keep Discord use in common spaces if possible, especially if they're navigating new social dynamics or emotional ups and downs after using it.

**Conversation Starters & Activities:** 

* To explore their interests and how they're using Discord to learn or grow: *"Are there any new things you've been getting into or learning about through Discord? I'd love to hear what's been fun or interesting for you lately."*
* To help them reflect on emotional boundaries: *"How do you usually feel after being on Discord—energized? Drained? Has anything ever made you want to leave a server or take a break?"*
* **Activity:** Have a weekly chat about what you're both enjoying or learning online. Your teen can share a Discord server they're into, and you can share something from your digital world too—whether it's a podcast you liked or a hobby you're exploring online. This makes it a shared conversation, not a one-sided check-in, and helps normalize thoughtful digital habits for both of you.

### Older Teens (15–17)

**What to Expect:** 

By this age, teens are likely using Discord as a major social outlet: managing multiple servers for different friend groups, hobbies, and identity-based communities. Gaming is still a central draw for many, and teens may use Discord to coordinate multiplayer games, talk strategy, or stream gameplay with friends. Others use it to explore creative projects, follow their favorite streamers, or talk about their favorite shows. They're increasingly independent and may seek more privacy in their digital spaces, but they'll still benefit from ongoing guidance. Emotional intensity, conflict, or exposure to distressing content can continue to affect their well-being, especially if they don't feel like they have a trusted adult to talk to.

**Safety Approach:** 

The goal is to support critical thinking, emotional boundaries, and positive digital habits (without micromanaging).

* Have regular conversations about how different online spaces make them feel, and what they need to do when a space stops feeling good.
* Revisit privacy and safety settings together after Discord updates to make sure they're still aligned with their values and needs.
* Normalize setting digital boundaries, like muting channels, taking breaks, or using the Ignore feature to protect their peace without escalating drama.
* Use Family Center only with mutual agreement, and frame it as a transparency tool—not a surveillance tool.
* Encourage reflection around how their online presence may impact future opportunities (college, jobs, leadership roles, etc.).
* Talk about balancing digital identities with real-life values: "*Does this server match who you are and what you care about?*"

**Conversation Starters & Activities:** 

* To explore identity, creativity, and values:*"What's one Discord server or group that really feels like **your** people? What makes it a space you want to come back to?"*
* To support emotional awareness and boundaries: *"Have you ever had to step back from a Discord conversation or server? What helped you know it was time to take a break?"*
* **Activity:**Do a "Digital Freaky Friday" swap. Ask your teen to pick a Discord server they think you'd enjoy and show you around. In return, share something you love, like a podcast, Pinterest board, meme account, or hobby space. Try doing this once a month. It keeps things fun and gives you both a way to stay connected while exploring each other's digital worlds.

## Making the Most of Discord

While Discord can come with risks, it also offers real opportunities for teens to connect, create, and grow. When used thoughtfully, Discord can be more than just a place to chat; it can be a space for learning, self-expression, and even friendship-building for teens.

**A few ways Discord can be a positive space for your teen:**

* They can connect with supportive communities around interests that may not be available in their school or local area.
* Many teens use it for study groups, collaborative projects, and homework help.
* Some libraries, classrooms, and educational programs now host Discord servers to support learning.
* Gaming servers can help teens build teamwork, problem-solving, and communication skills.
* For teens with social anxiety, text-based or voice-only communication can sometimes feel safer and less overwhelming than face-to-face interaction (​​but it shouldn't replace real-world support, professional help, or opportunities to build in-person social confidence over time).

### **How to Support Positive Use**

Instead of focusing only on limits, try helping your teen think more intentionally about how—and why—they're using Discord. Here's how:

* **Ask about what they enjoy**: Show interest in the servers they've joined and the types of conversations they're having.
* **Encourage exploration**: Suggest they look for servers focused on creative hobbies, STEM, mental health, books, or career interests.
* **Talk about digital citizenship**: Discuss how to be a kind, respectful, and constructive community member online—just like they would be in person.
* **Highlight real-world uses**: Let them know that people use Discord for things like school clubs, professional networking, creative collaboration, and even internships or job opportunities.
* **Find shared spaces**: Consider joining a family-friendly server together around a shared interest, like gaming, books, or a fandom. It can open up new ways to connect and model healthy use.
* **Bridge online interests to real life**: If they're part of a Discord server about art, gaming, writing, or another hobby, look for simple ways to bring that interest offline, like sketching, coding on free apps, joining a school club, or doing a DIY version at home. This can help balance screen time and make their digital world feel more connected to real life.

![purple blob](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_medium.png) [Back to top](#pug-view-links)

## A Note to Parents

Helping your teen navigate Discord—or any social platform—can feel like a lot. But **you don't have to get everything perfect**. What matters most is keeping the conversation going.

You know your child best. Age requirements are helpful guidelines, but you're the best judge of whether your teen is ready. And it's OK to say "not yet" if you feel they're not there yet—even if their friends are using it. That decision can be hard, especially if it leads to pushback or makes your child feel left out. But setting boundaries with care and staying open to future conversations can help ease that tension over time.

**Give yourself grace**. Digital parenting is something we're all figuring out as we go. It's OK to shift your approach as you learn more. What matters most is staying connected to your teen and being a trusted guide as they explore their online world.

For more support managing the challenges of digital parenting, check out our [Parents' Ultimate Guide to Managing Digital Parenting Anxiety.](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/articles/parents-ultimate-guide-to-managing-digital-parenting-anxiety)

# Parents' Ultimate Guide to Fortnite

### Are your kids caught up in the Fortnite frenzy? Here's everything you need to know about this popular video game.

[**What is Fortnite?**](#whatis)  
[**What is Fortnite: Battle Royale?**](#whatisbr)  
[**Do you play by yourself or with a team in Fortnite: Battle Royale?**](#team)  
[**What if I'm not ready for the action of Battle Royale?**](#whatifbr)  
[**What is Save the World?**](#stw)  
[**Why is my kid so interested in playing Fortnite?**](#whykids)  
[**Is Fortnite appropriate for kids?What age should kids be to play Fortnite?**](#appro)  
[**Are there parental controls for Fortnite?**](#parentalcontrols)  
[**Is Fortnite****too violent for kids?**](#violent)  
[**How much does Fortnite cost?**](#cost)  
[**What are Fortnite Seasons?**](#seasons)  
[**What are Fortnite Live Events?**](#live_events)  
[**What platforms can you play Fortnite on?**](#whatplatforms)  
[**How is Fortnite related to Twitch?**](#twitch)  
[**Can players chat with each other in Fortnite: Battle Royale?**](#playerchat)  
[**How do you turn off voice chat in Fortnite: Battle Royale?**](#voicechat)  
[**How long is a match of Fortnite: Battle Royale?**](#time)  
[**How do I manage screen time for my kids when they're playing Fortnite?**](#screentime)

## What is Fortnite?

If your kids say they're playing Fortnite, they're probably talking about [Battle Royale](/app-reviews/fortnite-battle-royale), the free-to-play multiplayer offshoot of the action-strategy game Fortnite from developer Epic Games. This ultra-popular video game blends elements of sandbox building games with fast-paced action. It offers two modes: a solo version called Save the World and the multiplayer version called Battle Royale. (Note: If you're looking for more parental insights on your kids' favorite things online, sign up for our [family movie night newsletter](/newsletters).)

## What is Fortnite: Battle Royale?

The game allows up to 100 people to participate in a match together. Players are dropped onto the game map and must compete to be the last one standing by killing every other player. During the game, players collect weapons, build safe structures, and try to avoid the Storm that damages all players outside of a safe zone. Players can also choose to play a no-build version, where you just focus on shooting people. Unlike the Save the World version, there aren't any zombies to kill, which makes it a less scary version to play. However, players can buy items to make themselves look like a zombie or another creepy character.

## Do you play by yourself or with a team in Fortnite: Battle Royale?

There are four modes of play in Battle Royale: Solo, Duo, Trio, and Team. In Solo mode, you're dropped into the game alone. In Duo, you're dropped in with one teammate, and in Trio, with two. In Team mode, you play on a team of four. Duos, Trios, and Teams can either be friends choosing to play together or randomly matched players. All players in a match are playing in the same mode.

## What if I'm not ready for the action of Battle Royale?

Don't worry if you've never played Fortnite or a battle royale game before. Playground mode lets players get used to the mechanics of the game without the pressure of fighting other gamers. Playground sessions are limited to a maximum of four players, and you can even put everyone on the same team to eliminate the possibility of friendly fire.

## What is Save the World?

Save the World is the traditional solo campaign in the game Fortnite. Unlike in Battle Royale, where players compete against each other, players in the Save the World mode are survivors of an apocalyptic storm where the few remaining humans must band together to defeat creepy zombie-like creatures called husks.

## Why is my kid so interested in playing Fortnite?

Kids love Fortnite for lots of reasons. One is that it combines two other genres that are big winners with young gamers. Another is that it has a more cartoonish look than some other more gory video games, so younger gamers are drawn to it.

Kids can play with friends in Duos, Trios, and Teams, creating a more social element. And popular gamers like play the game on streaming sites like YouTube and Twitch. Plus, in the case of the Battle Royale mode, it's free (although it does have in-app purchases—more on that below).

## Is Fortnite appropriate for kids? What age should kids be to play Fortnite?

For some parents, the cartoonish, bloodless style of the action in Fortnite makes the violence less problematic than the aggressive gore in other popular shooter games. But the game's online chat feature—especially in Battle Royale mode—could expose younger players to offensive language or mature content from random strangers. Common Sense recommends Fortnite for teens 13 and up, primarily because of the action violence. But with the [right controls](https://privacy.commonsense.org/evaluation/Fortnite) and parental guidance, this can be a preteen-friendly alternative to violent first-person shooters.

## Are there parental controls for Fortnite?

Yes, adults can restrict some features on their child's account. You can manage permissions for friend requests, voice and text chat, content ratings, and filters for mature language. Parents and caregivers can also set up passwords for in-game spending. When you enable this option, the Parental Control PIN will be required for all purchases. Accounts for users under 18 also have privacy settings turned on by default. [Use this guide](https://safety.epicgames.com/en-US/parental-controls) to set up parental controls on your child's account.

There is an additional restriction for kids under 13. Children below that age are automatically assigned a "[cabined account](https://www.epicgames.com/site/en-US/cabinedaccounts)," where parents and caregivers have to consent to their child getting access to certain features. These include in-game purchases and chatting. Keep in mind that the game determines a user's age based on the date of birth they enter when setting up an account.

## Is Fortnite too violent for kids?

Fortnite: Battle Royale is loaded with violence, but it's all cartoonish, rather than bloody or gory. Since the object is to be the last one standing, you'll constantly shoot other players and dodge fatal storms. However, there's no blood; defeated enemies simply vanish.

Those seeking a less violent—and more social—play experience can find it in the weapon-free Party Royale section, which you choose when you log in for a session. Party Royale has no killing and dying. Instead, the environment is more conducive to exploring environments while chit-chatting with friends and other players.

## How much does Fortnite cost?

Players can currently download and play Fortnite: Battle Royale for free. The current cost of Fortnite: Save the Worldis $39.99, although the developer, Epic Games, has suggested it will make it free or discounted some time in the future.

However, even within the free-to-play version, players can spend real money. Fortnite encourages purchases such as upgrades to Deluxe and Super Deluxe editions, as well as in-game currency called V-Bucks that can be used to buy bonus items.

The Premium Battle Pass requires a $10 subscription that lets players compete on more levels and win exclusive game skins/costumes. Epic's partnerships with popular entities including [Marvel](/articles/marvel-age-by-age-guide), [the Mandalorian](/tv-reviews/the-mandalorian), [Predator](/movie-reviews/predator), and [Tron](/search/tron) mean they frequently introduce new characters, costumes, and other crave-worthy elements—keeping players' interest up and their money coming in.

## What are Fortnite Seasons?

Unlike other multiplayer games, Battle Royale has a storyline, which results in frequent additions of new content to the game that are referred to as a new "season." Seasons seem to update approximately every 10–12 weeks, and 10 seasons make up a chapter. You'll begin to see clues to the updates during the current season, usually to encourage players to purchase the next season's Battle Pass.

## What are Fortnite Live Events?

The platform's live events, which are often tied to a feature in the game, can attract tens of millions of viewers (not just players) around the world. Some of the most popular events include concerts, such as ones by Marshmello, Travis Scott, and Diplo, as well as in-game promotional launches, such as director J.J. Abrams' release of an exclusive *Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker* trailer in advance of the movie.

Some of these events are scheduled and some are spontaneous. If your kid's into Fortnite, they'll probably hear the buzz and want to tune in. Events tend to be family-friendly and are listed in the [news section of the Fortnite site](https://www.epicgames.com/fortnite/en-US/news).

## What platforms can you play Fortnite on?

You can play Fortnite on the latest game consoles (PlayStation, Xbox, and Switch), computers (Mac and Windows), and [Android mobile devices](/app-reviews/fortnite-battle-royale). The one place you can't play it is on iPhones, since Epic Games [launched a very public battle against the Apple App Store](https://www.cnet.com/news/apples-battle-with-epic-games-could-lead-to-big-changes-in-iphone-apps/) over the way Apple collects in-app purchase fees—money Epic relies on, as it offers Fortnite: Battle Royale for free.

Users need an internet connection to play. Players can play "cross-platform," which means, for example, that a Windows player can be on a team with a console player. Gamers can also create an account on any device and carry over their progress in a game to another system. For example, you could start on a cellphone, then pick up a game on a computer or console later in the day and continue where you left off.

## How is Fortnite related to Twitch?

Some kids aren't only playing Fortnite—they're watching other people, including celebrities like Drake, play the game on Twitch. Twitch is a social media platform for gamers where they can livestream themselves playing popular video games, including Fortnite. Livestreaming can be unpredictable, so make sure to check out which gamers kids are watching, and if kids say they want to livestream themselves, carefully consider the risks.

## Can players chat with each other in Fortnite: Battle Royale?

Live, unmoderated chat is possible between users in the console and PC versions of Fortnite: Battle Royale. Options include voice chat and on-screen text chat. This exposes players to random strangers and the likelihood of profanity.

## How do you turn off voice chat in Fortnite: Battle Royale?

Open the Settings menu in the top right of the main Fortnite page by selecting the three bars, then the cog icon. Choose the Audio tab at the top of the screen. From there, you can adjust several audio features, including voice chat. Turn the setting from on to off by tapping the arrows.

## How long is a match of Fortnite: Battle Royale?

Each match in Battle Royale lasts about 20 minutes, although players who are killed early play for less time.

## How do I manage screen time for my kids when they're playing Fortnite?

When each match only takes 20 minutes, it's easy to fall into the trap of "just one more" ... sort of like how you end up binge-watching an entire season of [*Stranger Things*](/tv-reviews/stranger-things). But you can take advantage of the quick matches by using them as a natural stopping point in gameplay. Some kids benefit from using a timer, limiting themselves to a certain number of matches per day, or using one of [these tips for finding a balance between gaming and other activities](/articles/how-can-i-help-my-kids-develop-good-screen-time-habits).

Read Common Sense Media's [full review of Fortnite](/node/73828) and learn more about how it works.

*Jeff Haynes, former senior editor, web and video games, contributed to this guide.*

# Parents' Ultimate Guide to Snapchat

![blue and green abstract shapes](/themes/custom/common_sense/components/commonkit/atoms/ck-image/images/ratio_16_9_large.png)

## Parents Need to Know

* **Snapchat is a fast-moving, image-based app where most messages disappear.** Teens love it for casual, low-pressure communication—but that disappearing design can also make it harder to track bullying, risky content, and harmful behavior.
* **Most teens use Snapchat daily, and often feel pressure to stay constantly connected.** Features like Snapstreaks and real-time notifications are designed to keep them checking in, even when it's not healthy.
* **The app includes AI, group chats, location sharing, and a feature to hide sensitive photos.** Some tools, like My Eyes Only and My AI, may give teens a false sense of privacy or safety. Know what these features do and when they may be misused.
* **Teens can be exposed to risky content like sexting, drug offers, or pressure from strangers.** Disappearing messages and public Stories can make it easy for this to happen without parents knowing.
* **Safety settings and parental tools like Family Center help—but only when paired with open, ongoing conversations.** Settings can be changed by teens anytime, so building trust and regular check-ins matters more than surveillance.
* **Snapchat isn't just a risk—it can also be a space for creativity, connection, and family bonding.** Help your teen use it in meaningful ways, like private group chats with real friends, silly family Snaps, or creative storytelling with filters.
